title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
body_text: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH | Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry Home About AGITTOC 2020 2011-12 course 2014 course 2015-16 course 2017-18 course Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry November 20, 2026 Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH Posted by ravivakil under Uncategorized Leave a Comment   Hi everyone, I am at the American Mathematical Society Executive Committee and Board of Trustees meeting now, and about to chair an hours-long meeting, but this is urgent, so I will try to get this out quickly. Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it is so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft. I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is. Update about 8 hours later: I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.) title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
body_text: We promoted developers into architects without informing them Developer forever Home Posts About Contact Read my posts Read my posts All posts We promoted developers into architects without informing them Mani Doraisamy 9 hours ago 3 1 Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements: First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID. All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load. What is the right code for this? If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have: Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload. In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack. Why AI won’t push back AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen. Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app. Your new job is to architect AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to: Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code. That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability. If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding. Your future as developer In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you. 3 Like forum 1 share Share Comments · 1 Srinivasa Prasanna 5 hours ago Mani - could adopting a method like spec-driven development have helped here ? title: Levent Alpöge claims proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis [pdf]
Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
body_text: [2611.21885] Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Skip to main content Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.21885 (cs) [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Authors: Jiajun Fan , Neil He , Changyi Yang , Andy Mao , Xi Zhu , Chaoran Cheng , Kaiqu Liang , Shuaike Shen , Zetian Li , Ruihan Guo , Ge Liu View a PDF of the paper titled Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights, by Jiajun Fan and 10 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it. Contents paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf : the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026). lean/ : the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml ). lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2 and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper. lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved. The Lean package The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/ . Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean , names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice . To build, from lean/ : lake exe cache get lake build The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time. What is and is not here The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either. The source of the paper is not in this repository. State of the Lean text The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$ , one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled. About No description, website, or topics provided. title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
body_text: Unforced Euler singularity, unforced Navier-Stokes singularity, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis | What's new What's new Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao Home About Career advice On writing Books Mastodon+ Applets Subscribe to feed Unforced Euler singularity, unforced Navier-Stokes singularity, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis 20 November, 2026 in math.AP , math.NT | Tags: AI , incompressible Euler equations , Levent Alpöge , Matei Coiculescu , Navier-Stokes equations , Riemann hypothesis , Tristan Buckmaster | by Terence Tao Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are: Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions , which is formalized in Lean here . Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization . Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof. Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). (UPDATE: the moderators of the Lean thread are now focusing the discussion on the Lean-related aspects of the proof only.) I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task. See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results. Response: You should sit down. Reply 20 November, 2026 at 3:39 pm Anonymous And why should he be surprised? Riemann perhaps could be, but why Hilbert if formalization of mathematics was his idea, the idea of a “thinking machine” goes back to Leibniz and the theoretical notion of a Turing machine was introduced 7 years before Hilbert’s death? This may be surprising to us, because it happened so quickly, we knew the visions of AI from sci-fi books and at the same time we were aware of the failures of previous approaches to formal theorem proving, but c’mon in 2443? Reply 20 November, 2026 at 9:49 am Science Markets Thank you for the ordering by how digested the results are. That ordering is the whole story, and it is worth being explicit about why. For the first two results the digestion path is already visible: human-readable proof, strategy broadly clear, Lean formalisation on top. A reader can form a judgement in an afternoon. The third has no such path yet. A Lean-only artifact of that size is a different kind of object, and the question “is it right” splits into questions that resolve on very different timescales: does the headline statement in Lean say what we mean by GRH; does the archive compile against a known-good Lean with only standard axioms; is the strategy something a number theorist recognises as a proof. The Zulip thread can answer the second relatively quickly. The third is the one that has always taken years. The two precedents are both uncomfortable. Wiles announced in 1993, the gap surfaced within months, and the repair took until 1995. Mochizuki published in a refereed journal in 2012 and the people who work on the problem still do not accept it. In neither case could the answer be read off the artifact. Which makes the interesting question not “is it true” but “what observable event would settle it, and who is entitled to say so”. For anyone trying to price this rather than just follow it, writing that down before the claim exists is the only version that is worth anything. Written afterwards it collapses into an argument about credibility, which is precisely the failure mode this whole episode is about. Disclosure: I work on https://science.markets , which runs a market on this question. The resolution rule is fixed before the market opens and cannot be edited: https://science.markets/markets/riemann-zeta-critical-line/ — it requires a complete unconditional proof in ZFC, independently checked with no unresolved gap, and it says in advance that finite numerical verification does not count and that independence from ZFC leaves it unresolved. Being forced to write down what does not count was the useful part. Someone has to say it out loud, and it is probably better coming from inside the house. The recent wave of formal Lean proofs from Anthropic—culminating in the claim regarding the Riemann Hypothesis—marks the end of pure mathematics as a level playing field. For centuries, math was the ultimate equalizer: a mind with a chalkboard had the same tools as a professor at Princeton. Now, it looks much more like Formula 1. You can be the best driver in the world, but if a competitor works for a factory team and gets to drive the unreleased prototype—the car the public won’t see for another two years—they are going to set the track record. An objective look at recent results makes it hard to argue that narrow human mastery is still the main bottleneck. Levent Alpöge has been resolving long-standing conjectures in fields well outside his own specialization. While steering these systems clearly requires mathematical maturity, the fact that one researcher can break open unfamiliar subfields shows that the underlying engine is now compensating for—and in some cases outperforming—decades of niche human expertise. To be clear, the fact that a machine can prove theorems is not surprising in itself. We have always known that mathematics can be formalized, and in principle, a computer could stumble upon a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis purely by luck. In that sense, it is not fundamentally different from chess—just vastly more complex, where trying every possible path of formulas is far too demanding to be feasible. What is genuinely astonishing is not that computers can prove deep results, but how rapidly the technology has evolved to navigate that immense search space and consistently choose viable paths toward a proof. There is, however, a gentle historical irony in how we got here. For generations, parts of our community maintained a quiet intellectual hierarchy. In textbook margins and conference coffee breaks, we have all heard the playful—and sometimes not-so-playful—jokes about physicists, computer scientists, and especially engineers, portraying them as a bit sloppy or heuristic-driven. It was always a slightly misplaced sense of superiority; step outside our own technical niches and talk to most of us about any everyday topic, and we are rarely any more insightful than anyone else. Yet look at who actually built the machine now tackling the pinnacle of pure mathematical rigor: not a department of 500 pure mathematicians, but a lab guided by physicists’ empirical scaling laws, designed by computer scientists, and built by thousands of veteran software, systems, and hardware engineers—who then handed the keys to a handful of mathematicians. In fact, perhaps the most positive outcome of this shift is that AI is bringing a healthy dose of humility back to the mathematical community. Watching empirical engineering and large-scale compute break into what we long treated as the exclusive fortress of pure human genius is a grounding, and probably overdue, reality check. Pure mathematics is no longer a solo marathon of raw intellect. It has become a constructors’ championship—and the most urgent question for academia is how open research survives when the fastest engines remain behind corporate doors. P.S. To be clear, this isn’t directed at Terence Tao or mathematicians in general—only at that small, overly elitist corner of the culture we have all encountered at some point. I write this as an established research mathematician with no personal axe to grind—just someone who has always known that an engineer can possess the exact same deductive power as any brilliant mathematician; it is only the methods and the language that differ. title: The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
body_text: Shtetl-Optimized » Blog Archive » The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis Shtetl-Optimized The Blog of Scott Aaronson If you take nothing else from this blog: quantum computers won't solve hard problems instantly by just trying all solutions in parallel. Also, please read Zvi Mowshowitz's masterpiece on how to fix K-12 education! --> « More podcasts, conversations, talks The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis “… it is very probable that all roots are real. Of course one would wish for a rigorous proof here; I have for the time being, after some fleeting vain attempts, provisionally put aside the search for this, as it appears dispensable for the immediate objective of my investigation.” –Bernhard Riemann, 1859 [ Update: According to “Poe’s Law,” there is no irony or sarcasm on the Internet so obvious that it won’t fly over countless people’s heads. In line with that, lots of people on social media are now saying variants of “how dare Scott Aaronson call LLMs ‘stochastic parrots,’ that demeaning and trivializing term from 2021? Doesn’t he understand that these so-called ‘stochastic parrots’ just proved the Riemann Hypothesis?” ROFL.] I’m in California to visit Oratomic and then Inkhaven . I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis , producing 17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code . At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis? Still several more years?” I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore. After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are at most 3/8 away from the critical line ( Quanta just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have. So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly? For those tuning in from home, the Riemann Hypothesis says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n). While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous Prime Number Theorem ), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger. David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?” Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him. Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand. They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement! All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now. I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates have needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand. Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean.  They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves.  And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds.  And while they’re working on it, how many more such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors? My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point. Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things. The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will anything last that we currently take for granted? It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation: Dana: I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to… Me: Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months. This leak… Dana: We should still fix the leak. Follow This entry was posted on Friday, November 20th, 2026 at 12:29 pm and is filed under AI , The Fate of Humanity . You take away public key cryptography right now and the internet becomes wild west. You have credit cards, banks, stock market, all relying on secure communications. title: Restricting AI agents in mobile operating systems platforms from capturing data
body_text: Signal >> Blog >> Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy Get Signal Help Blog Developers Our Mission Give Now Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy Meredith Whittaker on 20 Nov 2026 Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it. This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data. We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. 1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. 2 The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission. In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding. The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation. So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. 2 People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem. We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS. 3 We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us. We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on: Developers should have an easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing, including (but not limited to) screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, all without undermining the core utility of an application. Operating system companies should create better documentation and technical specifications around how these AI agents function, particularly regarding data access and processing. Confidential computing approaches are not a complete solution, and do not address these core concerns. In particular, these approaches still leave the power to determine the extent of privacy guarantees (if any) in the hands of these providers. We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents. In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry. Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes . We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights. Signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization. Microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩ There are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing users), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩ 2 Careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 users is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. ↩   Tweet Facebook Don't have Signal? Additionally, in training the model, we trained on absolutely no copyrighted recordings. the model is open source and you can use its outputs for commercial purposes. 60.8 56.1 47.4 45.7 composite 70.8 67.1 57.0 58.2 onsets 79.1 75.7 71.2 63.9 frames 40.9 40.1 31.4 30.5 offsets 52.5 41.4 30.1 30.0 drums dettato 20M mirelo A2M v1.1 pro muscriptor 1.3B yourmt3+ 46M the composite, and the measures it is the mean of, for each system system composite onsets frames offsets drums parameters dettato 60.8 70.8 79.1 40.9 52.5 20M Mirelo A2M v1.1 Pro 56.1 67.1 75.7 40.1 41.4 not published MuScriptor 47.4 57.0 71.2 31.4 30.1 1.3B YourMT3+ 45.7 58.2 63.9 30.5 30.0 46M sets used: PHENICX , RWC classical, RWC royalty-free F1 per set: the mean of onset, frame and offset dettato mirelo A2M v1.1 pro muscriptor 1.3B yourmt3+ Bach10 91.3 Dagstuhl ChoirSet 60.8 PHENICX-Anechoic 64.8 RWC Popular 54.0 RWC Classical 64.4 RWC Genre 48.7 RWC Jazz 55.7 RWC Royalty-Free 61.6 Slakh2100 (synthetic) 68.4 20 40 60 80 100 F1 per set: the mean of onset, frame and offset set dettato mirelo A2M v1.1 pro muscriptor 1.3B yourmt3+ Bach10 91.3 not reported 54.7 57.9 Dagstuhl ChoirSet 60.8 not reported 35.5 28.0 PHENICX-Anechoic 64.8 60.9 54.4 44.8 RWC Popular 54.0 not reported 44.3 36.1 RWC Classical 64.4 65.8 58.4 62.4 RWC Genre 48.7 not reported 42.6 35.6 RWC Jazz 55.7 not reported 52.0 47.1 RWC Royalty-Free 61.6 56.2 46.8 45.4 Slakh2100 (synthetic) 68.4 not reported 51.1 not reported disclaimer with the benchmarks: it's difficult to gauge the true accuracy of the model for your use-case without trying it yourself. one thing my model performs poor on for instance, is splitting instruments correctly. If you're looking for something that you can actually play(e.g sheet music), i'd reccommend songscription or klangio - both are excellent tools by great companies that push the envelope of what's possible in this field forward. the stars and stripes forever swan lake rachmaninoff mendelssohn bugablue intro first strain second strain trio breakstrain piccolo solo breakstrain again grandioso loading 0:00 / 0:00 recording dettato sousa, the stars and stripes forever: “the president's own” united states marine band, from the complete marches of john philip sousa, vol. 3. a us government recording, public domain. download the MIDI upload your own example (or pick a demo below) run audio to midi the driving goal of kobimusic: to help musicians, not replace them. a part of that goal means following copyright law. we trained dettato on a mix of synthetic instrument recordings and CC solo instruments mixed in using the URMP dataset. the rest of the instruments morph together ~20 soundfonts, using the 'soundfont babies' technique i published. no copyrighted recordings were used. I began working on dettato about 10 months ago, but scrapped what I had in about April. The reason why was that I treated AMT as a data problem - but in reality, the bottleneck is architecture. There are a lot of parellels that you can draw for OMR (first model i made) and AMT . both traditionally were tackled early on using algorithms. later, in both fields they plugged in giant LLM components. These models would naturally become overfit to synthetic data, since globally the problems of AMT and OMR become different than if you treat it locally. But, for both you can reframe it as a local problem. For OMR , using a detector model. For AMT , a pitch-lane model. overall, i hope both open and closed weight music retrieval companies can learn from this. title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
body_text: Introducing Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed, and verified end-to-end by AI | Architect Labs Architect Labs Home Blog About Careers Get in touch → Get in touch → Privacy Policy © 2026 Architect Silicon Inc. Architect Labs ← Back to Posts Introducing Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed, and verified end-to-end by AI Research November 18, 2026 Abstract In our previous post, Redwood , we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?” Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core. Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts. Introduction to interaction nets Mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly. Interaction nets 1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine 2 compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3 Fig. 1. Five queens, two ways. On the left, a C++ program walks the search tree one step at a time. On the right, the same search as an interaction net explores many branches at once: 3,183 interactions with a critical path of only 262 steps. Fig. 1 shows the difference on a small search problem, placing five queens on a five-by-five board. The sequential program visits one candidate at a time. The interaction net exposes all of its independent work: on average, about twelve interactions are ready to run at every step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get this parallelism; the dependencies were simply never thrown away. In theory, this should have two large advantages. The first is multithreading for free: rather than varying levels of coarse and fine-grained parallelism, parallelism comes straight from the program. No threads, locks, or race conditions, and none of the out-of-order machinery a conventional core uses to dig it back out. The second is that, since every value has one owner and every step is local, data can live in small local memories next to where it is used. That removes much of the area and power a conventional chip spends on large caching subsystems, and much of the system-level complexity of keeping those caches coherent. Process Frostbite was designed with zero architectural priors. We followed the process below, riding multiple agent swarms along the way. Fig. 2. The Frostbite program from first proposal to ablations: key events, the stages of work, and the worktrees the agents created, with each branch drawn in its phase's color. Architecture exploration and selection To begin architectural exploration, we had to establish the set of workloads Frostbite should do exceedingly well in. We decided to look at different ways a program could expose its work: many independent pieces at once, rounds of parallel work, long sequential chains, data-dependent branches, and recursion. Under each category, we created a search set and a held-out eval set to evaluate the final Frostbite on, ensuring the design generalized to programs it was never tuned on. The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work. Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression. Fig. 3. All 25 workloads, grouped by how each program exposes its work, and split into the search set the agents tuned on and the held-out eval set, with the size each was run at. Agents synthesized research papers and existing benchmarks, and built Python models to trade off high-level architectural ideas against each other, before narrowing to a single architectural concept. The output of this exploration was a 141-page PDF covering the proposed programming model, the runtime, and the high-level blocks of the chip. This was nowhere near the final architecture, but rather a starting point where all the prior findings, high-level requirements, constraints, experiments, and runtime traits were described. Once the first architectural iteration completed (first RTL generation), this was deleted, since many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible. Formal contracts and system modeling Once the architecture candidate was selected, our system moved on to building the full software model of the chip. Building software models is essential when exploring an architectural space, as they allow fast iteration between the workloads, the ISA, and the abstracted view of the hardware. Whether we build a CPU, GPU, NPU, or networking switch, mastering this iteration loop allows the fastest exploration of the design space within a finite time. To do this repeatedly, we designed a new in-house specification language, ASL, and wrote Frostbite's system model “Arcmodel” in it. ASL supports machine-checkable translations and refinements between RTL, system models, UVM, SVA, and more, all against a formally backed specification. Its power and performance estimates are accurate to within 1–5%, it runs roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation, and it is formally verifiable through “contracts.” In every silicon program to date, human architects have written many English PDFs before handing off to an implementation team and a verification team. However, natural language cannot capture every detail an implementation needs precisely and unambiguously, and it cannot guarantee that every agent hallucination is caught while the ASIC is being designed and verified. Natural language was never built for this, and in a world where AI writes the specification, we opt for a formal, machine-checkable specification language instead. ASL can formally describe both high-level, protocol-like behavior, such as out-of-order handling, CSR programming, memory ordering, and coherency, and low-level details, such as pipelines, arbitration mechanisms, and compute transfer functions. This lets the model leave the specification open-ended where that is useful and constrain it exactly where a precise behavior is required. ASL also translates natively to Lean, 4 which we use for all theorem proving when checking AI outputs across RTL, UVM, C, SVA, and more. We will discuss ASL in more detail in a future post. Throughout the entire development of Frostbite, our AI iterates on the Frostbite ISA, Arcmodel, Design, and Verification tightly together, maintaining the ASL Contract as the source of truth. We've found that having a single, provable source of truth prevents a large class of bugs, silly mistakes, and reward-hacking instances when deploying large agent swarms. Ultimately, this common language allows the models to work across the stack nimbly, reflecting the changes propagated from the workload down to the final hardware. By the end, our Frostbite ASL lowered down to 800k+ lines of Lean. Fig. 4. The Lean contracts of all 31 blocks. Each block is a cluster of what its contract names, joined by what reads what and, in blue, by the signals blocks share. Below, we zoom into the Frame Manager (FRM) block. RTL and alignment Because ASL is a formally backed specification, designing and verifying the RTL derived from it is the fastest part of the entire Frostbite process. Arcmodel, however, is not physically aware, so its power and performance estimates at first diverge from the true numbers of the timing-converged, synthesis-clean RTL, in the worst case by almost 250%. Before continuing the ASL autoresearch, one of our systems recalibrates Arcmodel against the RTL. This is a fully autonomous pipeline. It first identifies the power hotspots in the RTL and traces them down to key counters in the formal specification, such as SRAM reads and writes, operation counts, flits sent and received, credit returns, and frame misses. The model may then write any scalar Python function over those counters to predict power, and it repeats this process until the RTL and Arcmodel agree to within 5%. We find this style of non-gradient learning extremely powerful. Once this first physical alignment has been applied, later iterations are much faster. These are, of course, still pre-silicon power numbers, and over multiple tapeout loops, ASL models can be correlated to true post-silicon, production power numbers. Fig. 5. Error between modeled energy and RTL energy over the program. The Python models stayed far from the RTL; after the first power fit, Arcmodel was realigned and searched until its error fell into the 1–5% band. By aligning the Arcmodel and RTL so closely, the continued swarms were able to explore and exploit much faster. The full Arcmodel chip simulations are much faster than the RTL (660x faster), which led to many cross-stack optimizations. For instance, our AI systems discovered very fine-grained clock gating tricks, and adjusted the software runtime accordingly to accommodate them in a matter of hours. Such a cross-stack optimization is near-impossible to execute on in a traditional ASIC flow. Contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power, iterated together Once Arcmodel and the RTL agreed, the original Python models and the architecture PDF were deleted, and the ASL contracts became the only specification of the chip. From then on, contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power moved forward together. Swarms of agents proposed architecture revisions in parallel worktrees; each change was checked against the contracts, modeled in Arcmodel, implemented in RTL, and measured for power, and then either kept or dropped. Across four searches and a final round of ablations, the swarm tried 58 ideas and kept 37 of them, from clock gates on a running tile to smaller L3 tables and one shared expander. Fig. 6. From the first release to the end of the program, drawn out: each search's ideas, the worktrees they became, and the agents working on them, with every idea kept or dropped. Architectural novelty The architecture in full detail would warrant its own post. Instead, we choose to focus here on the features that we considered either novel or creative and highlight the capability of our systems to push the frontiers of hardware design. Programs for Frostbite are written in Vine, 2 which is a fully fledged programming language with syntax similar to Rust. A Vine program is compiled to Ivy , an intermediate representation (IR) that encodes the interaction net structure. The optimizer also tries to apply as many of the graph reduction rules as it can, so the final Ivy net , as it is called, has a (mostly) fixed shape, composed of three primitives: data, computation nodes, and control nodes. However, the runtime of this net is still very dynamic, because unlike the typical computation graph, where the parallelism is encoded in the structure and pipelined over time, the parallelism has to be derived at runtime from the state and pipelined spatially . The initial naïve implementations were slow, so our agents had to get creative. The generated ISA follows from this set of constraints. A lot of it is expected: wide bundles, hardware loop counters, and streams. We found the dynamic features more interesting, particularly operations to take, peek, and copy values from other parts of the net that would be running in parallel. The tiles then come alive, communicating across space. Fig. 7. Code-to-hardware on Frostbite. The first call populates the chip, and then the calls it makes follow it, reusing the same nodes in a recursive fashion, until every tile is firing at once. The recursion is spread across space. Emergent property: stealing work Because the parallelism is spread over space, there is no central scheduler. Instead, we saw the agents design these elegant rules for propagating the work. A tile follows three rules: it runs its own work first, meaning work in its input ports. If those are empty, it takes work from a neighboring tile that has work to spare. If no such tile is found, it can just go inactive and save power. The agents demonstrated remarkable sophistication in how they implemented this. Below, we have the hardware for a single Frostbite tile: Fig. 8. A Frostbite tile. The bounding boxes demonstrate how to think about the domains of the blocks. A lot of them should be familiar. We are interested in the RUNTIME domain that is responsible for the work-stealing behavior described above. The compiler breaks code into short sections that run uninterrupted once their inputs are ready. These are run in the engine and are mostly organized like traditional computation through the front end . Whenever a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces whose sizes aren't known ahead of time, the running section parks whatever comes after into a small record in local memory, the frame manager . It then drops the new tasks onto a hardware queue called the work queue and picks up the newest one itself. Idle neighbors are then free to pull the remaining tasks over the network. As tasks finish anywhere on the chip in any order, their return packets tick down the parked record's counter and automatically wake the next section the instant the last piece arrives. This is what it looks like in hardware: Fig. 9. How tiles share a workload. We can think of each “task” as the current board, one level down, with one more queen. Tile 0 has to queue three tasks for all the possible queen configurations before it can finish the present board state. It's free, so it takes the newest task (from itself) and runs it. Meanwhile, its neighbors have gotten the other ones, except for Tile 5, which goes back to sleep. This behavior was never specified by any human. We can directly trace it back to necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics. Results We synthesized Frostbite on a 7 nm process, reaching 800 MHz timing at synthesis and 500 MHz in the final GDS. Each Frostbite quad (a two-by-two grid of tiles) paired with four L3 nodes is 0.792 mm². We benchmark one Quad+L3 cluster against a single core of a modern superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU, which we refer to as TCPU (“Traditional CPU”). This TCPU is 0.895 mm² at the same process. † Fig. 10. Frostbite layout, four by four tiles, on a 7 nm process, with one Frostbite quad (two by two tiles) and one L3 node outlined. We benchmarked on a wide set of workloads, from dense, parallel kernels such as gemm and conv2d, to irregular, branching programs such as JSON parsing, Huffman coding, k-d trees, and recursive Fibonacci. A search set of workloads drove all architectural optimization, ISA design, RTL, and verification, and the chip was evaluated on both the 10 search-set workloads and the 15 held out, including the five practical workloads added later (Fig. 3). For a fair comparison, we chose to first measure “single-core” performance by benchmarking one Frostbite quad against the TCPU, since they have similar area. Across all the workloads, we average an 8.77x performance-per-area, and across all 25 workloads, search set and held out together, Frostbite reaches a geometric mean of 4.59x the TCPU's performance-per-watt: 6.02x on the 10 search-set workloads, and 3.83x on the 15 held-out workloads it was never tuned on. As expected, the architecture does most strongly on highly parallelizable tasks, but it also outperforms the TCPU on branching, dynamic code. Fig. 11. Performance-per-watt of one Frostbite quad relative to the TCPU's best build, across 25 workloads: the 10 in the search set, and the 15 in the held-out eval set. Dashed lines mark the geometric mean of the eval set, of all 25, and of the search set. Fig. 12. Share of each chip's energy by function, excluding clock distribution, for the TCPU, one Frostbite quad, and the full four-by-four Frostbite. Mean over 20 workloads. The energy breakdown shows where the savings come from. Leaving out clock distribution (49% of TCPU energy, 41% of a Frostbite quad's), the TCPU spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Frostbite cuts memory to 38% and fetch, decode, and issue to just 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on its on-chip network and scheduler, the cost of sharing work and moving messages between tiles. What's more exciting, however, is that as we scale the chip to a four-by-four array (four quads), the power distribution is relatively the same. In a general-purpose multi-core CPU arrangement, scaling the number of cores requires adding heavy coherency mechanisms and large caches, whereas when running interaction nets, the same data locality rules always apply, and more cores do not increase system complexity. This is illustrated below. In the coming months, we'll be benchmarking Frostbite mesh-like configurations against multi-core “TCPU” arrangements with large caches and larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs, over a larger set of industry benchmarks such as SPEC and PARSEC. Fig. 13. Where the memory sits. A multi-core TCPU shares a deep hierarchy of L1, L2, and L3 caches across its cores; Frostbite gives every tile its own small memory. Schematic, not to scale. What comes next While interaction nets have been around for more than 35 years, their production value has never been fully clear. Historically, there has always been a risk of exploring out-of-distribution architectures, for the time, investment, and labor required to come to conviction. We believe AI fundamentally changes these economics. In the search for higher performance and lower power, extreme co-design of workloads, ISA, and hardware will continue to be demanded. With large agent swarms, sophisticated search-space techniques, precise guardrails, formal verification, and faster EDA tools, AI systems will be able to discover and build novel accelerators at a quality that exceeds human cognition. While there is much more to do, we feel it is the right time to share with the world what the future of autonomous chip design could look like. We plan to continue scaling development on Frostbite, including but not limited to: Deliver a software playground for anybody to run a program on Frostbite, hosted on FPGAs. Build a preliminary operating system capable of managing hardware resources, multiple programs, virtualization, and more. Scale swarms to bring Frostbite to higher performance-per-watt, and benchmark it on a much larger set of workloads against a broader set of CPUs. Release the RTL and ISA for Frostbite. We are having a lot of fun! Notes † For legal reasons, we cannot disclose the exact CPU. References 1 . Lafont, Y. (1990). “Interaction Nets.” Proceedings of the 17th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL ’90), 95–108. doi:10.1145/96709.96718 2 . The Vine programming language. vine.dev 3 . Tendrils (2026). “On Interaction Nets.” tendrils.co/blog/2026-04-26/on-inets 4 . de Moura, L., and Ullrich, S. (2021). “The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language.” Automated Deduction – CADE 28, LNCS 12699, 625–635. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 Partner with us If your edge depends on the silicon underneath it, whether you're an AI lab, a fabless chip company, an OEM, a defense prime, or ASIC design partner, we want to hear from you.
