title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
body_text: Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in the physics of black holes \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude 01 Introduction Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes 01 Introduction 02 A note about Claude’s methods 03 The Hawking-Page transition 04 The modular bootstrap 05 Conclusion Published Nov 17, 2026 Team Science Topics Discovery Agents Reasoning Beneficial Deployments See more... Related articles Science Nov 4, 2026 Investigating vault particles with Claude View more Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously. This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave. The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits. To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics. This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future. The modular bootstrap As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim. As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10 -35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality. Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one. Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model , a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems. In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own. Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies. To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension. Three possible shapes of spacetime in 3D gravity: a ball, a donut (or torus), and a two-holed donut. The spacetime is the inside of each shape, and the quantum theory is “written” on its surface. The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus . There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time. Two ways to interpret the same donut-shaped spacetime. (left) Time runs the long way around the hole, and space is represented by the shorter loop; (right) space runs the long way around, and time is represented by the shorter loop. In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment. Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer. If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out. The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories? This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin. Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question. Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve . Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper. This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search. Conclusion These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research. Read the black hole phase transition paper here , and the modular bootstrap paper here . title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
body_text: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it · cekrem.github.io cekrem.github.io learnelm.dev Jesus!? About Recommended Books Podcast (🇳🇴) Blog If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it November 20, 2026 4-minute read AI • Software Craftsmanship • Coding-as-Craft Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice . This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all , and has never really been. Except in software engineering, somehow. When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing . Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield 1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.” Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all. To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose !? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills. “There’s more to software engineering than writing code” Link to heading Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service! ), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change. Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you? So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing! Which brings me to my next point: All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems Link to heading if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems . And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it , then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error ), and very few are learned without effort at all . Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea . It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? — Em’s blog 2 , emphasis mine. Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar!   ↩︎ I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great!  ↩︎ © 2021 - 2026 Christian Ekrem

title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
body_text: If you can’t explain something in simple terms, you don’t understand it KOTTKE DOT ORG KOTTKE DOT ORG MENU Member Login Home Membership Newsletter Goods Search Archive + Tags About/Contact dark mode light mode Advertise here with Carbon Ads Socials & More Newsletter RSS Feed Bluesky Mastodon This site is made possible by member support . 💞 Big thanks to Arcustech for hosting the site and offering amazing tech support. When you buy through links on kottke.org, I may earn an affiliate commission. Thanks for supporting the site! kottke.org. home of fine hypertext products since 1998. Beloved by 86.47% of the web. 🍔   💀   📸   😭   🕳️   🤠   🎬   🥔 × close posted Jun 15, 2017 by Jason Kottke  ·  gift link If you can’t explain something in simple terms, you don’t understand it In the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics . Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture . From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 issue of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine : Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.” John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well: Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely. Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine , rubber bands , how trains go around curves , and magnets . Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets , he says: I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with. Feynman was also quoted as saying: I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics. Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read: What I cannot create, I do not understand. The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending. Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock() . I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock() . No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int , but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths. Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c , which rejected only len > INT_MAX . I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod . Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client . I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable ( env:VAR ), otherwise the command line will be too long. Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840 . Checklist documentation is added or updated tests are added or updated --> Sorry, something went wrong. Uh oh! title: Do not buy RAM, compress
body_text: Do not buy RAM, compress! | Therry van Neerven Home Services Contact Blog en Do not buy RAM, compress! 19 Nov, 2026 AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram , a solution to compress memory. Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled. Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4. I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. This could have cut our Cloud spend in half! How it looks in practice I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics) for u in nos.nl nu.nl telegraaf.nl ad.nl volkskrant.nl nrc.nl rtl.nl tweakers.net buienradar.nl ns.nl npo.nl \ bbc.com/news edition.cnn.com theguardian.com nytimes.com reuters.com apnews.com aljazeera.com dw.com spiegel.de lemonde.fr washingtonpost.com bloomberg.com \ theverge.com arstechnica.com techcrunch.com wired.com engadget.com phoronix.com lwn.net news.ycombinator.com tomshardware.com \ github.com/torvalds/linux github.com/microsoft/vscode github.com/rust-lang/rust stackoverflow.com/questions gitlab.com developer.mozilla.org docs.python.org kernel.org ubuntu.com huggingface.co \ youtube.com "youtube.com/results?search_query=linux" "youtube.com/results?search_query=music" "youtube.com/results?search_query=documentary" twitch.tv vimeo.com dailymotion.com soundcloud.com open.spotify.com \ reddit.com reddit.com/r/linux reddit.com/r/worldnews reddit.com/r/pics reddit.com/r/technology x.com instagram.com linkedin.com pinterest.com tumblr.com imgur.com 9gag.com medium.com quora.com \ bol.com coolblue.nl marktplaats.nl amazon.nl amazon.com ebay.com aliexpress.com ikea.com/nl/nl zalando.nl etsy.com mediamarkt.nl ah.nl \ google.com/maps openstreetmap.org booking.com airbnb.com tripadvisor.com klm.nl schiphol.nl \ en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nederland \ imdb.com rottentomatoes.com archive.org nationalgeographic.com nasa.gov flickr.com/explore espn.com weather.com \ canva.com figma.com notion.so trello.com office.com dropbox.com wikihow.com ; do firefox --new-tab "https:// $u " >/dev/null 2 > & 1 ; sleep 1 done If we look at the running apps, then we see it should not fit. In the memory usage we see that some demand was placed into the zram swap space. In the terminal we can check how much memory is used, and we can calculate the compression ratio. 5.7G of data in 1.7G of RAM. That’s a compression ratio of 1:3.35. Getting started with zram compression Compressing RAM is something which helps to get you more out of your own hardware, but also out of your cloud environment. Do more with less. The Arch Linux wiki has a good article on how to get started . Looking forward to hearing about your experiences. Update (20 November 2026) zram is nice, but zswap is better! Yesterday the article got featured on Hacker News . Nice to see the conversation and I hope that some of you started experimenting with compressing memory. Making more efficient use of the available resources is something important to understand as a community. Two articles were mentioned that I think are a very important addition. While zram works fine for my situation, they advocate that zswap is the better option for most situations. After reading both articles I agree with this conclusion. So, I will be changing my configuration to use zswap instead. Make sure to read the following: I was wrong! zswap IS better than zram by Hayden James, in Blog Linux Debunking zswap and zram myths by Chris Down Get in touch Looking to hire a software engineer or technical leader for your project? title: PostgreSQL 19
body_text: PostgreSQL: Release Notes Home About Download Documentation Community Developers Support Donate Your account November 19, 2026: PostgreSQL 19 Released! Quick Links Documentation Manuals Archive Release Notes Books Tutorials & Other Resources FAQ Wiki Release Notes PostgreSQL 19.0 E.1. Release 19 Prev   Up Appendix E. Release Notes Home   Next E.1. Release 19 # E.1.1. Overview E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 E.1.3. Changes E.1.4. Acknowledgments Release date:  2026-11-19 E.1.1. Overview # PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including: New REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table. pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies plan advice automatically based on the query. Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations. Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica . Logical replication of sequence values . Support for “ read-your-writes ” consistency on standbys via the new WAIT command. Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a new scoring system. The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below. E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 # A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to new major releases. Version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities: Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) § The default warning period is seven days. Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) § The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings . MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18. Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) § PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP , which is unfixably insecure. Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) § Dumps created using pre- PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall , and using standard_conforming_strings = off , will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on . Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off , for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary. Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) § pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems. Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § § The btree_gist inet / cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet / cidr indexes. Disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) § The values of such columns were not well-defined. Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) § This previously returned NULL . Cause transactions to pass their READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) § This means READ ONLY transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions. Change default of max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas) § Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases. Remove server variable io_workers (Thomas Munro) § This has been replaced by four new variables; see Section E.1.3.1.2 . Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) § Previously JIT was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable JIT . Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) § Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by vacuum_cost_limit . With this change, VACUUM with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases. Rename column sync_error_count to sync_table_error_count in system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Vignesh C) § This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately. Rename wait event type BUFFERPIN to BUFFER and rename wait event BufferPin to BufferCleanup (Andres Freund) § Remove wait event BufferContent and add more precise wait events BufferShared , BufferShareExclusive , and BufferExclusive (Andres Freund) § Change index access method handlers to use a static IndexAmRoutines structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) § Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) § Change psql 's \crosstabview command to honor the \pset null setting (Chao Li) § Change full text search and pg_trgm to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) § Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., ICU , builtin ) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the LC_CTYPE setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of C , the output of some full text search and pg_trgm functions could change. When upgrading such databases using pg_upgrade , it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and pg_trgm after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored tsvector values. Change how fuzzystrmatch functions handle non- ASCII characters (Peter Eisentraut, Jeff Davis) § § dmetaphone() and dmetaphone_alt() now upper-case their input using the database's default collation rather than always using libc, and soundex() , metaphone() , and difference() now treat only ASCII letters as letters. When upgrading with pg_upgrade , it is recommended to reindex any indexes that use these functions after the upgrade. Remove MULE_INTERNAL encoding (Thomas Munro) § This encoding was complex and rarely used. Databases using it will need to be dumped and restored with a different encoding. E.1.3. Changes # Below you will find a detailed account of the changes between PostgreSQL 19 and the previous major release. E.1.3.1. Server # E.1.3.1.1. Optimizer # Allow NOT IN clauses to be converted to more efficient ANTI JOIN s when NULLs are not present (Richard Guo) § Allow more LEFT JOIN s to be converted to ANTI JOIN s (Tender Wang, Richard Guo) § Allow use of Memoize for ANTI JOIN s with unique inner sides (Richard Guo) § Allow some aggregate processing to be performed before joins (Richard Guo, Antonin Houska) § § § This can reduce the number of rows needed to be processed. Improve hash join's handling of tuples with NULL join keys (Tom Lane) § Improve the planning of semijoins (Richard Guo) § Allow Append and MergeAppend to consider explicit incremental sorts (Richard Guo) § Convert IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM NULL to IS [NOT] NULL during constant folding (Richard Guo) § The latter form is more easily optimized. Simplify IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM to equality/inequality operators when inputs are proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) § Perform earlier constant folding of var IS [NOT] NULL in the optimizer (Richard Guo) § This allows for later optimizations. Simplify COALESCE() and ROW(...) IS [NOT] NULL to avoid evaluating unnecessary arguments (Richard Guo) § § Simplify IS [NOT] TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN to plain boolean expressions when the input is proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) § Speed up join selectivity computations for large optimizer statistics targets (Ilia Evdokimov, David Geier) § Add proper optimizer statistics for functions returning boolean values (Tom Lane) § Allow extended statistics on virtual generated columns (Yugo Nagata) § Allow function pg_restore_extended_stats() to restore optimizer extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier, Chao Li) § § § § Add function pg_clear_extended_stats() to remove extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) § Adjust the optimizer to consider startup costs of partial paths (Robert Haas, Tomas Vondra) § Allow negative values of pg_aggregate . aggtransspace to indicate unbounded memory usage (Richard Guo) § This information is used by the optimizer in planning memory usage. E.1.3.1.2. General Performance # Improve performance of foreign key constraint checks (Junwang Zhao, Amit Langote, Chao Li) § § Improve asynchronous I/O read-ahead scheduling for large requests (Andres Freund) § § § Allow io_method method worker to automatically control needed background workers (Thomas Munro) § The new server variables are io_min_workers , io_max_workers , io_worker_idle_timeout , and io_worker_launch_interval . Allow query table scans to mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map (Melanie Plageman) § Previously only VACUUM and COPY ... FREEZE could do this. Allow autovacuum to use parallel autovacuum workers (Daniil Davydov) § § The maximum number of workers is controlled by server variable autovacuum_max_parallel_workers and per-table storage parameter autovacuum_parallel_workers . Allow TID Range Scans to be parallelized (Cary Huang, David Rowley) § Improve COPY FROM performance for text and CSV input using SIMD CPU instructions (Nazir Bilal Yavuz, Shinya Kato) § Improve NOTIFY to only wake up backends that are listening to specified notifications (Joel Jacobson) § Previously most backends were woken by NOTIFY . Change wal_compression equals on to use the best WAL compression method available (wenhui qiu) § Previously this always used pglz . Change the default TOAST compression method from pglz to the more efficient lz4 (Euler Taveira) § This is done by changing the default for server variable default_toast_compression . Improve performance of internal row deformation (David Rowley) § Improve performance of repeated UTF-8 case-folding operations (Andreas Karlsson) § Improve performance of hash index bulk-deletion and GIN index vacuuming using streaming reads (Xuneng Zhou) § § Improve sort performance using radix sort (John Naylor) § Improve timing performance measurements (Lukas Fittl, Andres Freund, David Geier) § § This benefits EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING) and pg_test_timing , and is controlled via server variable timing_clock_source . Optimize plpgsql syntax SELECT simple-expression INTO var (Tom Lane) § E.1.3.1.3. System Views # Add system view pg_stat_lock and function pg_stat_get_lock() to report per-lock-type statistics (Bertrand Drouvot) § Add system view pg_stat_recovery to report recovery status (Xuneng Zhou, Shinya Kato) § § Add system view pg_stat_progress_repack to report the progress of REPACK , CLUSTER , and VACUUM FULL (Álvaro Herrera) § Add system view pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to report per-table autovacuum details (Sami Imseih) § Add vacuum initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_vacuum (Shinya Kato) § The new started_by column reports the initiator of the vacuum, and mode indicates its aggressiveness. Add analyze initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_analyze (Shinya Kato) § The new started_by column reports the initiator of the analyze. Add system view pg_dsm_registry_allocations to report dynamic shared memory details (Florents Tselai, Nathan Bossart) § § Add mem_exceeded_count column to system view pg_stat_replication_slots (Bertrand Drouvot) § This reports the number of times that logical_decoding_work_mem was exceeded. Add slot synchronization skip information to pg_stat_replication_slots and pg_replication_slots (Shlok Kyal) § § § The new columns are slotsync_skip_count , slotsync_last_skip , and slotsync_skip_reason . Add update_deleted column to system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Zhijie Hou) § This reports the number of rows where updates were ignored due to concurrent deletes. This requires the subscriber have retain_dead_tuples enabled. Add sync_seq_error_count column to system view pg_stat_subscription_stats to report sequence synchronization errors (Vignesh C) § § Add stats_reset column to system views pg_stat_all_tables , pg_stat_all_indexes , and pg_statio_all_sequences (Bertrand Drouvot, Sami Imseih, Shihao Zhong) § It also appears in the sys and user view variants. Add stats_reset column to system views pg_stat_user_functions and pg_stat_database_conflicts (Bertrand Drouvot, Shihao Zhong) § § Add location column to system views pg_available_extensions and pg_available_extension_versions to report the file system directory of extensions (Matheus Alcantara) § Add backup_type column to system view pg_stat_progress_basebackup to report the type of backup (Shinya Kato) § Possible values are full or incremental . Add connecting value to system view column pg_stat_wal_receiver . status (Xuneng Zhou) § Add reporting of the bytes written to WAL for full page images (Shinya Kato) § This is accessible via system view pg_stat_wal and function pg_stat_get_backend_wal() . Add information about range type extended statistics to system view pg_stats_ext_exprs (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) § E.1.3.1.4. Monitoring # Allow log_min_messages log levels to be specified by process type (Euler Taveira) § The new format is type : level . A value without a colon controls all process types, allowing backward compatibility. Add server variable log_autoanalyze_min_duration to log long-running analyze operations by autovacuum operations (Shinya Kato) § Server variable log_autovacuum_min_duration now only controls logging of vacuum operations by autovacuum. Enable server variable log_lock_waits by default (Laurenz Albe) § Add server variable debug_print_raw_parse to log raw parse trees (Chao Li) § This is also enabled when the server is started with debug level three and higher. Make messages coming from remote servers appear in the server logs in the same format as local server messages (Vignesh C) § These include replication, postgres_fdw , and dblink servers. Add reporting of WAL full-page write bytes to VACUUM and ANALYZE logging (Shinya Kato) § Add IO wait events for COPY FROM/TO on a pipe, file, or program (Nikolay Samokhvalov) § Add wait events for commit_delay and for WAL write and flush LSN s (Xuneng Zhou) § § Have pg_get_sequence_data() return the sequence page LSN (Vignesh C) § Add function pg_get_multixact_stats() to report multixact activity (Naga Appani) § Issue warnings when the wraparound of transaction IDs or multixacts is less than 100 million away (Nathan Bossart) § The previous warning was 40 million. Warnings are issued to clients and in the server log. E.1.3.1.5. Server Configuration # Add scoring system to control the order that tables are processed by autovacuum (Nathan Bossart) § The new server variables are autovacuum_freeze_score_weight , autovacuum_multixact_freeze_score_weight , autovacuum_vacuum_score_weight , autovacuum_vacuum_insert_score_weight , and autovacuum_analyze_score_weight . Add server-side support for SNI (Server Name Indication) (Daniel Gustafsson, Jacob Champion) § New configuration file PGDATA/pg_hosts.conf specifies hostname/key pairs. Allow OAuth validators to register custom pg_hba.conf authentication options (Jacob Champion, Zsolt Parragi) § Allow roles pg_read_all_data and pg_write_all_data to read/write large objects (Nitin Motiani, Nathan Bossart) § These roles are designed to allow non-super users to run pg_dump . Allow background workers to be configured to terminate before database-level operations (Aya Iwata) § This allows database-level operations to complete more quickly since blocking background workers can now be terminated. Allow server variables that represent lists to be emptied by setting the value to NULL (Tom Lane) § Update GB18030 encoding from version 2000 to 2022 (Chao Li, Zheng Tao) § See the commit message for compatibility details. E.1.3.1.6.  Streaming Replication and Recovery # Add WAIT command to allow standbys to wait for LSN values to be written, flushed, or replayed (Kartyshov Ivan, Alexander Korotkov, Xuneng Zhou) § § Improve function pg_sync_replication_slots() to wait for replication synchronization completion (Ajin Cherian, Zhijie Hou) § Previously, certain synchronization failures would not be reported. Add server variable wal_sender_shutdown_timeout to limit replica synchronization waits during shutdown (Andrey Silitskiy, Hayato Kuroda) § By default, senders still wait forever for synchronization. E.1.3.1.7.  Logical Replication # Allow sequence values stored in subscribers to match the publisher (Vignesh C) § § § This occurs during ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... [ADD|SET|REFRESH|DROP] PUBLICATION . Function pg_get_sequence_data() allows inspection of sequence synchronization. Allow CREATE / ALTER PUBLICATION to publish all sequences (Vignesh C, Tomas Vondra) § This is enabled with the ALL SEQUENCES clause. Allow ALTER SUBSCRIPTION on publications to synchronize the existence of sequences on subscribers to match the publisher (Vignesh C) § This is enabled with the REFRESH SEQUENCES clause. Allow CREATE / ALTER PUBLICATION to exclude some tables (Vignesh C, Shlok Kyal) § § § § This is controlled with the EXCEPT clause, and is useful when specifying ALL TABLES . Add CREATE / ALTER SUBSCRIPTION setting retain_dead_tuples to retain information needed for conflict detection (Zhijie Hou) § § § Also add setting max_retention_duration to limit retain_dead_tuples retention. Allow CREATE SUBSCRIPTION to use postgres_fdw foreign data wrapper connection parameters (Jeff Davis) § The connection parameters are referenced via CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... SERVER . When server variable wal_level is replica , allow automatic enablement of logical replication when needed (Masahiko Sawada) § New server variable effective_wal_level , application pg_controldata , and function pg_control_checkpoint() report the effective WAL level. Allow wal_receiver_timeout to be set per-subscription and user (Fujii Masao) § § This allows subscribers to use different wal_receiver_timeout values. RETURNING (Andreas Karlsson, Marko Tiikkaja, Viktor Holmberg) § This allows conflicting rows to be returned, and optionally locked with FOR UPDATE / SHARE . title: "I can tell you wrote this yourself"
body_text: "I can tell you wrote this yourself" – Em's Blog Em's Blog Home Blog What I'm Doing Now Photo Guestbook "I can tell you wrote this yourself" 19 Nov, 2026 Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project. It's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that. I accidentally set the due date for the report a week early in my calendar, so after spending 48 hours stressed and pumping out 5,000 words, citing references and adding diagrams 1 , I was pleasantly relieved to find I'd tricked myself into being quite productive. I had a lot of time to get my supervisor to review the report and action his feedback. When he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it. A compliment? An insult? Then he followed it up with: "I've been sent a lot of reports written by AI." At first this shocked me. Our reports are limited to 10 pages - so the appendices are getting a big workout around here - how hard is it to write 10 pages yourself? But then I thought about what the last year of my engineering degree has been like. Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day. The reason why we've been pushed to use it? Apparently it's the way the industry is going. Apparently actually knowing things doesn't matter nearly so much as knowing how to prompt a machine to do the thing. Apparently the future of engineering - at least in my field - is to become a glorified babysitter. The AI isn't going anywhere, they say, so it's best we learn how to manage it well. But sitting in a room telling an AI "ignore the approaching deadline, we still have 8 hours, keep working" isn't exactly filling me with enthusiasm for the rest of my career. It's soul crushing, and I don't want to outsource so much of my thinking to it. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don't want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can't help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea. It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? Because I worry that it starts with using it for an assignment when you're encouraged to, but then it turns into relying on it to write a 10-page report on a project you should know back-to-front. A project that you'll have to present and defend in person when it finishes. And then you're asking it for advice, using it to summarise books, turning to it for anything you would normally look up or ask a friend. The internet is riddled with AI content that is making it increasingly more difficult to tell fact from fiction. In a world where everything is so polarised and deliberately provoking, the ability to identify bias or motivation in the content we consume has perhaps never been more important. Being able to think for ourselves has perhaps never been more important. As the tech world continues to offer us increasingly more opportunities to automate things, I'm practically begging you to please not automate your thinking. Read the books. Write the papers. Search for answers instead of asking AI. Ask a friend. Ask your mum about the mystery illness you're convinced you're developing and then take her advice and try drinking a glass of water. Think about what the creators of the content you consume want you to think 2 . Treat the things you consume like the Year 7 English class where you were taught how to identify persuasive techniques. Think about things as much as possible. Please just don't get the AI do it for you. On a more positive note, here's some recent good things: Got to see a tawny frogmouth up close recently - in the middle of the day! One has nested in a tree near the university's engineering precinct. Finished my final assessment for the semester today! Officially only one semester to go! Went and saw 'You Can See Everything' with Han last week and I can't stop talking and thinking about it. If you've seen it, please talk to me about it. If you haven't seen it, please go and see it! Felt homesick the other day and made Mum's scalloped potatoes recipe! SO good. The weather has been beautiful lately. Morning runs and walks have been extra fun. The other morning I ran past a guy walking barefoot through the park with a CAT in his backpack. Made plans with Bec & Han to see 'Sunrise On The Reaping' next Monday - no spoilers if you've already seen it! Keen to talk about it after then. Anyhow, happy almost-weekend! -- Em Subscribe to my blog LaTeX is painful. ↩ I think what I want you to think here is probably pretty obvious. ↩ Toast this post   Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ
