title: What's New in PHP 8.6
body_text: PHP: PHP 8.6 Release Announcement Downloads Documentation Get Involved Help English Русский 简体中文 Nederlands Français Italiano Brazilian Portuguese 日本語 Search docs PHP 8.6.0 Released! Getting Started Introduction A simple tutorial Language Reference Basic syntax Types Variables Constants Expressions Operators Control Structures Functions Classes and Objects Namespaces Enumerations Error Handling Fibers Generators Attributes References Explained Predefined Variables Predefined Exceptions Predefined Interfaces and Classes Predefined Attributes Context options and parameters Supported Protocols and Wrappers Security Introduction General considerations Installed as CGI binary Installed as an Apache module Session Security Filesystem Security Database Security Error Reporting User Submitted Data Hiding PHP Keeping Current Features HTTP authentication with PHP Cookies Sessions Handling file uploads Using remote files Connection handling Persistent Database Connections Command line usage Garbage Collection DTrace Dynamic Tracing Function Reference Affecting PHP's Behaviour Audio Formats Manipulation Authentication Services Command Line Specific Extensions Compression and Archive Extensions Cryptography Extensions Database Extensions Date and Time Related Extensions File System Related Extensions Human Language and Character Encoding Support Image Processing and Generation Mail Related Extensions Mathematical Extensions Non-Text MIME Output Process Control Extensions Other Basic Extensions Other Services Search Engine Extensions Server Specific Extensions Session Extensions Text Processing Variable and Type Related Extensions Web Services Windows Only Extensions XML Manipulation GUI Extensions Keyboard Shortcuts ? This help j Next menu item k Previous menu item g p Previous man page g n Next man page G Scroll to bottom g g Scroll to top g h Goto homepage g s Goto search (current page) / Focus search box Released November 19, 2026 Faster, Safer, More Powerful. PHP 8.6 is a major update of the PHP language , with new features including Partial Function Application , a new Duration class, a Polling API , and a new clamp() function What's new in 8.6 Upgrade to PHP 8.6 Key Features in PHP 8.6 More expressive code , stronger types , and scalable I/O . Partial Function Application Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, returning a Closure that accepts the rest. New \Time\Duration Class The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Polling API Scalable I/O multiplexing using epoll, kqueue, and other native mechanisms, available to event loop libraries like ReactPHP and AMPHP. New clamp() Function Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. New SortDirection Enum A standard, type-safe way to express sort order that can be shared across libraries. Readonly Property Defaults Allows readonly properties to declare default values, so fixed values no longer have to be assigned in the constructor. Partial Function Application Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, using ? and ... placeholders for the rest. The result is a Closure, and the function is only called once the remaining arguments are passed to it. PHP 8.5 and older $versions = [ '8.4' , '8.5' , '8.6' , '8.7' , '9.0' ]; $supportsPfa = array_filter ( $versions , fn ( $version ) => version_compare ( $version , '8.6' , '>=' ), ); PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ $versions = [ '8.4' , '8.5' , '8.6' , '8.7' , '9.0' ]; $supportsPfa = array_filter ( $versions , version_compare (?, '8.6' , '>=' ), ); New \Time\Duration Class The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Its representation is independent of any time and timezone and can represent a range of more than 250 years with nanosecond precision. This makes it well-suited to represent timeouts or benchmark timings in an expressive way. PHP 8.5 and older /** * All delays are in microseconds. */ function backoff ( int $baseDelay , int $step , int $attempt , ): void { $delay = $baseDelay + ( $step * ( 2 ** $attempt )); // Wait at most 30 seconds. usleep ( min ( $delay , 30_000_000 )); } // 1 second base delay, plus 100 milliseconds // doubling with each attempt. backoff ( 1_000_000 , 100_000 , $attempt ); PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ use Time\Duration ; function backoff ( Duration $baseDelay , Duration $step , int $attempt , ): void { $delay = $baseDelay -> add ( $step -> multiplyBy ( 2 ** $attempt )); // Durations are comparable, so min() works directly. $delay = min ( $delay , Duration :: fromSeconds ( 30 )); time_nanosleep ( $delay -> seconds , $delay -> nanoseconds ); } backoff ( Duration :: fromSeconds ( 1 ), Duration :: fromMilliseconds ( 100 ), $attempt , ); // Preconfigure the delays using Partial Function Application. $waitBeforeRetry = backoff ( Duration :: fromSeconds ( 1 ), Duration :: fromMilliseconds ( 100 ), attempt : ?, ); $waitBeforeRetry ( $attempt ); Polling API The new Io\Poll API efficiently monitors many streams at once using the best mechanism available on each platform (epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll), without the scalability limits of stream_select() . It is designed as a common foundation that event loop libraries such as ReactPHP and AMPHP can build on. PHP 8.5 and older $server = stream_socket_server ( 'tcp://0.0.0.0:8080' ); $clients = []; while ( true ) { $read = [ $server , ... $clients ]; $write = $except = null ; // Based on select(), which typically can't handle // more than 1024 connections stream_select ( $read , $write , $except , null ); foreach ( $read as $stream ) { if ( $stream === $server ) { $clients [] = stream_socket_accept ( $server ); continue; } $data = fread ( $stream , 8192 ); if ( $data === '' || $data === false ) { $key = array_search ( $stream , $clients , true ); unset( $clients [ $key ]); fclose ( $stream ); } else { fwrite ( $stream , $data ); } } } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ use Io\Poll \{ Context , Event }; $server = stream_socket_server ( 'tcp://0.0.0.0:8080' ); // Automatically uses epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll $poll = new Context (); $poll -> add (new StreamPollHandle ( $server ), [ Event :: Read ]); while ( true ) { foreach ( $poll -> wait () as $watcher ) { $stream = $watcher -> getHandle ()-> getStream (); if ( $stream === $server ) { $client = stream_socket_accept ( $server ); $poll -> add ( new StreamPollHandle ( $client ), [ Event :: Read ], ); continue; } $data = fread ( $stream , 8192 ); if ( $data === '' || $data === false ) { $watcher -> remove (); fclose ( $stream ); } else { fwrite ( $stream , $data ); } } } Stream Error Handling Stream operations can now be configured to throw a StreamException or to fail silently instead of emitting warnings. Errors are reported as structured StreamError objects with a StreamErrorCode enum case, the wrapper name, and the affected path or URL, and can also be retrieved later with stream_last_errors() or passed to a custom error handler. PHP 8.5 and older $config = @ file_get_contents ( '/etc/app/config.json' ); if ( $config === false ) { // Only an unstructured message string is available $error = error_get_last (); log_error ( $error [ 'message' ]); } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ $context = stream_context_create ([ 'stream' => [ 'error_mode' => StreamErrorMode :: Exception , ], ]); try { $config = file_get_contents ( '/etc/app/config.json' , context : $context , ); } catch ( StreamException $e ) { foreach ( $e -> getErrors () as $error ) { // $error->code is a StreamErrorCode enum case log_error ( $error -> code -> name , $error -> message , $error -> wrapperName , ); } } New clamp() Function Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. Otherwise, the nearest boundary value is returned. PHP 8.5 and older var_dump ( max ( 0 , min (- 10 , 100 ))); // int(0) var_dump ( max ( 0 , min ( 50 , 100 ))); // int(50) var_dump ( max ( 0 , min ( 110 , 100 ))); // int(100) PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ var_dump ( clamp (- 10 , 0 , 100 )); // int(0) var_dump ( clamp ( 50 , 0 , 100 )); // int(50) var_dump ( clamp ( 110 , 0 , 100 )); // int(100) // Any comparable value works with clamp(). This // includes the new Duration class. var_dump ( clamp ( \Time\Duration :: fromSeconds ( 30 ), min : \Time\Duration :: fromMinutes ( 1 ), max : \Time\Duration :: fromMinutes ( 10 ), )-> seconds ); // int(60) New SortDirection Enum The SortDirection enum provides a shared, type-safe way to express sort order with its Ascending and Descending cases. Previously, every library had to define its own way of representing sort direction, resulting in a mix of incompatible integers, strings, booleans, and custom enums. Since SortDirection is built into PHP, libraries can accept it in their public APIs without needing adapter code. Learn more about this feature in The PHP Foundation’s blog . PHP 8.5 and older class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy ( string $column , int $direction = SORT_ASC , ): static { $this -> orderBy [] = $column . ' ' . match ( $direction ) { SORT_ASC => 'ASC' , SORT_DESC => 'DESC' , }; return $this ; } } $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_DESC ); $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_STRING ); // Accepted by the signature, then fails inside the method: // UnhandledMatchError: Unhandled match case 2 PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy ( string $column , SortDirection $direction = SortDirection :: Ascending , ): static { $this -> orderBy [] = $column . ' ' . match ( $direction ) { SortDirection :: Ascending => 'ASC' , SortDirection :: Descending => 'DESC' , }; return $this ; } } $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SortDirection :: Descending ); $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_STRING ); // TypeError: QueryBuilder::orderBy(): Argument #2 ($direction) // must be of type SortDirection, int given DocComments for Function Parameters Function and method parameters can now have their own DocComments, which are available via the new ReflectionParameter::getDocComment() method. This allows each parameter to be documented right next to its declaration, without repeating its name and type in a @param tag. PHP 8.5 and older class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. * * @param string $query Terms to search * @param int $limit Maximum number of results */ public function search ( string $query , int $limit = 10 ): array { return []; } } // Parameter descriptions can only be extracted // by parsing the function's DocComment. PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. */ public function search ( /** Terms to search */ string $query , /** Maximum number of results */ int $limit = 10 , ): array { return []; } } var_dump ( new ReflectionParameter ([ DB ::class, 'search' ], 'query' ) -> getDocComment (), ); // string(22) "/** Terms to search */" New ReflectionProperty::isReadable() and ReflectionProperty::isWritable() Methods With readonly properties, asymmetric visibility, and property hooks, checking whether a property is public is no longer enough to know whether it can be read or written. The new methods answer this directly for a given scope, and optionally for a specific object, taking into account visibility, initialization state, hooks, and magic methods. PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ class NewsEntry { public string $title = 'PHP 8.6 released!' ; public private(set) string $slug = 'php-86-released' ; } $entry = new NewsEntry (); foreach ([ 'title' , 'slug' ] as $item ) { $property = new ReflectionProperty ( NewsEntry ::class, $item ); printf ( "%s: isReadable=%s isWritable=%s\n" , $item , $property -> isReadable ( null , $entry ) ? 'yes' : 'no' , $property -> isWritable ( null , $entry ) ? 'yes' : 'no' , ); } // title: isReadable=yes isWritable=yes // slug: isReadable=yes isWritable=no Readonly Property Defaults Instance readonly properties, including those in readonly classes, can now declare a default value. This makes it simple to implement get-only interface properties with fixed values, which previously required assigning them in a constructor. The default counts as the property's initialization, so the constructor cannot overwrite it. PHP 8.5 and older interface Rule { public string $parser { get ; } } final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule { public string $parser ; public function __construct () { $this -> parser = SlugParser ::class; } } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ interface Rule { public string $parser { get ; } } final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule { public string $parser = SlugParser ::class; } Additional Features and Improvements The #[\Override] attribute can now be applied to class constants and enum cases. Enums can now implement the __debugInfo() magic method. Properties of objects stored in constants can now be modified directly, e.g. Config::DEFAULTS->timeout = 30 . New Uri\Rfc3986\UriBuilder and Uri\WhatWg\UrlBuilder classes build URIs from their components, along with new methods for detecting URI and host types and a Uri\WhatWg\url_percent_encode() function. The Sodium extension adds post-quantum key encapsulation (X-Wing and ML-KEM-768), IP address encryption, and the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE extendable-output functions. TLS streams now support session resumption, external pre-shared keys, and TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT). New mysqli::quote_string() method escapes a string and wraps it in quotes, matching PDO::quote() . pack() and unpack() now accept the < and > endianness modifiers on integer and float format codes. JSON error messages now include the location of the error in the input. The new error_include_args INI setting consistently includes function arguments in error messages. New grapheme_strrev() function reverses strings by grapheme cluster, and the new IntlNumberRangeFormatter class formats ranges of numbers. New ZipArchive::openString() and ZipArchive::closeString() methods work with in-memory archives. Performance improvements include compiling array_map() with first-class callable or partial application callbacks into loops, faster printf() calls, caching of stateless closures, and faster JSON encoding. Deprecations and Backward Compatibility Breaks Using return inside a finally block is now deprecated, as it silently discards exceptions and overrides values returned from the try or catch block. Returning a value from __construct() or __destruct() is now deprecated, as is making them generators. Declaring a nullable return type for __debugInfo() is also deprecated. Using let or is as the name of a class, function, or constant is now deprecated. Using _ as a constant name, namespace as a class constant name, or readonly as a function name is also deprecated. The mbstring regular expression functions such as mb_ereg() and mb_split() have been deprecated, as the underlying Oniguruma library is no longer maintained. PCRE functions with the u modifier can be used instead. The is_double() , is_long() , is_integer() , and doubleval() aliases have been deprecated. Use is_float() , is_int() , and floatval() instead. spl_object_hash() has been deprecated in favor of spl_object_id() , and spl_classes() in favor of ReflectionExtension::getClassNames() . Passing an object where an array is expected to array_walk() , array_walk_recursive() , http_build_query() , mb_convert_variables() , and compression functions and filters is now deprecated. Use get_object_vars() to convert the object first. strcoll() and the SORT_LOCALE_STRING sort flag have been deprecated. Use the Collator class from the intl extension instead. Passing a third argument to define() is now deprecated, as is calling is_a() or is_subclass_of() with a class name string when $allow_string is false . Using more than 16 filters in a php://filter URL without setting the filter.max_filter_count context option is now deprecated. Sessions are now more secure by default: session.use_strict_mode and session.cookie_httponly are enabled, and session.cookie_samesite is set to Lax . Custom session handlers that do not implement both create_sid() and validateId() are now deprecated. The metaphone() , mysqli_get_charset() , and mysqli_stmt_init() functions are now deprecated, along with the CSV methods of SplFileObject and the sorting, flag, and serialization methods of ArrayIterator . trim() , ltrim() , and rtrim() now also strip form feed ( \f ) characters by default. fclose() , file_put_contents() , and copy() now return false when flushing or closing the stream fails, instead of silently ignoring the failure. Many functions now throw a ValueError for out-of-range values, invalid flags, or strings containing NUL bytes, instead of silently truncating or ignoring them. Better syntax, improved performance and type safety. Upgrade to PHP 8.6 The full list of changes is recorded in the ChangeLog . Please consult the migration guide for a detailed list of new features and backward-incompatible changes. PHP is developed and maintained by a global community of contributors. The PHP Foundation helps fund this work. If PHP is part of your business or projects, consider sponsoring the Foundation. title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
body_text: UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order Home Field Notes Sightings About Contact Donate Fellow Anorak Search Sign in Subscribe Field Notes UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency. MacAnorak 19 Nov 2026 5 min Share There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all. That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 , which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice . This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat. I covered the background to this extensively in my piece, Two-Tier Encryption in the UK . The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging not just to users in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law. Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information. [1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services . They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so. The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice , but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice , this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026 . The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs. At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute” . The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument. As Reuters reports , the Tribunal concluded: “The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.” The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret. In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government. Alice had enabled Advanced Data Protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users , Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection. Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature. Our iCloud accounts contain a lot of private information — photos, documents, backups, other material that most of us reasonably expect to remain fully private. Encryption exists so that the service provider shouldn't have the ability to access that information. If a government can compel a technology company to undermine its own protections, the consequences deserve considerably more scrutiny than secret exchanges between officials and lawyers. Today's ruling makes scrutiny more possible. The Investigatory Powers Act doesn't only exist to regulate Apple's relationship with the UK government. Its provisions establish powers that can potentially be applied to other communications and technology providers. What happens when these powers are used against another company? What happens when the next notice concerns a different service or a different encryption system, or a different category of personal information? How would customers even know about it anyway? That's one of the most troubling aspects of the TCN regime - the secrecy . Companies receiving TCNs can be legally prohibited from disclosing that they have received them. The UK government’s position, of course, is that these powers are necessary to support lawful investigations and protect public safety. Liberty and Privacy International have thankfully been challenging the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of this regime. They argue it lacks adequate safeguards and threatens fundamental rights. Apple is pursuing its own legal challenge. These cases are now proceeding alongside one another with a substantive hearing expected sometime in 2027. Today's decision doesn't resolve the wider questions, but it does remove one obstacle to examining the dispute in public. Apple has consistently argued that it will not build ‘backdoors’ into its products. The UK government, meanwhile, has relied on powers that allow it to issue orders to technology companies in secret. For now, the legal process has at least established that the government issued this particular order, but my guess is that we're still some distance from fully understanding what it actually wants Apple to do, and whether it has the legal authority to demand it. I will continue to follow this one very closely indeed. Advanced Data Protection is not synonymous with all iCloud data encryption. Apple already encrypts various categories of iCloud information without ADP, but some of those categories remain accessible to Apple and can potentially be provided in response to valid legal demands. ADP changes that arrangement by extending end-to-end encryption to additional categories of data. ↩︎ Read next A Wolf at the Door: Apple Is Rethinking Mac Permissions for the Age of AI Agents Following the furore surrounding Meta’s Muse and the appetite of AI agents for access to our personal data, Apple promised to tighten macOS privacy controls. Now we know what it’s planning. MacAnorak 18 Nov 2026 The MacBook Pro’s OLED PWM Problem: When a ‘Better’ Display Becomes Worse to Use Apple has made a spectacular display. But spectacular isn’t the same as comfortable, and the people discovering that distinction deserve to be heard. MacAnorak 14 Nov 2026 Some M5 Macs Are Struggling With High-Refresh-Rate Displays. Is Apple’s Graphics Pipeline Broken? What began as a scrolling problem with Apple’s Studio Display XDR is now being reported across multiple M5 Macs and external displays. Users report that their M6 machines don’t suffer from the same problems. MacAnorak 08 Nov 2026 Subscribe to MacAnorak Become a Fellow Anorak and get my Field Notes directly delivered to your inbox. title: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
body_text: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? · Kernel kernel Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? November 2026 Y Discussion on Hacker News ▲ 238 points 125 comments → While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes: Time and cost per trial Left is faster; lower is cheaper. API list price On a $200 plan, fully used Carbon is priced at its post-introductory rate. Subscription subsidization rates used: Opus 40×, Astra 13×, Carbon 3×, Hydrogen 17×. Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this. Theo - t3.gg @theo I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage. Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s Nov 11, 2026 828 104 replies Elliot Arledge @elliotarledge i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things Nov 12, 2026 36 5 replies Shayan @ImSh4yy dude why is carbon so fucking slow Nov 13, 2026 8 4 replies Simon Mahns @ CoRL @nautsimon_ carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it Nov 16, 2026 30 3 replies To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness. The Task In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes. Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop. Slow inference, or more work? The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes: Seconds per step Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show: The workload GPT-6 Astra against Gemini 4 Carbon, mean per bug. GPT-6 Astra Gemini 4 Carbon lighter = lower effort Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input. Ruling out the obvious Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations. The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference. Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix. Reading the traces We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work: Semantic trace analysis Each model’s steps, grouped by what they were for. Leaves out the 20 steps Carbon spent re-reading code it had already read; the next section covers those. Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for: Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch. Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported. Can Carbon identify its own overworking? Sample trial: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit Minutes from the start of each run. GPT-6 Astra at max effort, Gemini 4 Carbon at high. In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes. Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?" Sample trial with check-ins: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit The same bug and scale as above. Gemini 4 Carbon at high, with the check-in injected every five turns (circles). With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows. Carbon's necessary work is also slower Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen. Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime. Conclusion On difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources: Slower inference. Each step takes longer, which explains 16–30% of the gap against Astra and about half against Opus. Unnecessary work. About half of Carbon's steps went on work the tickets never asked for: auditing code the fix didn't need and closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Mechanical inefficiencies. Fewer tool calls per step and frequent re-reading slow Carbon down; we estimate that fixing them alone would cut its runtime by roughly a quarter. title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
body_text: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite - Zerodha Tech Blog Home Blog Projects Stack Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite 19 Nov 2026 Sarat Chandra Software Engineer TLDR; We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency. On Kite , our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes. Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB ( ssdb ), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years. Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement: SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable. Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads. As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were: A key-value blob store with a simple API. Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets. Horizontally scalable, distributed. Disk-space efficiency / compression. Easily maintainable and highly economical. So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following: ScyllaDB: We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB. PostgreSQL: We already have considerable experience with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as BYTEA columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency. YugabyteDB: Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features. RocksDB: Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes. Ceph: Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out. SeaweedFS: This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts. S3 and MinIO: Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Not to mention, S3 would incur significant costs given thousands of ops per second and tens of millions of ops per day. Raw filesystem (one file per blob): Putting blobs directly on disk meant implementing atomic writes and write batching, managing large numbers of files and directories, good old atomic read/write disk performance and inode headaches, and maintaining a separate metadata index for TTLs. Not to mention, orchestrating this over AWS storage volumes. Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens? So we ended up building Blobasaur , an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB. What we needed We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements: Redis protocol compatibility (if possible at all): Every existing client already used standard Redis libraries ( GET , SET , HGET , HSET , DEL , EXPIRE ). If we could get a system that could be a drop-in replacement, that would allow us to leave existing services untouched and reduce risk significantly. Low latency across payload sizes: It needed to serve both 2 KB settings blobs and 5 MB chart layouts with single-digit millisecond latency. Built-in compression: Almost all our payloads are repetitive JSON, which compresses well. Simple CRUD with TTLs: We didn’t need complex data structures, server-side scripting, or secondary queries. We just needed key-value and hash CRUD with key expiry. Multi-node partitioning: We needed to split data across multiple machines so a single node wasn’t a bottleneck. Relaxed durability is acceptable: This store holds non-critical UI and workspace preferences, and not critical financial data. If a sudden power loss drops recent writes, a user might lose a recent chart layout tweak, which is annoying, but it never affects trading. This was a good performance trade-off for our use case. Why SQLite (and Rust) We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves: Atomic writes and batching. TTL cleanup, which needs secondary indexes or walking the directories. Dealing with fd limits. Managing metadata separately from the raw data. SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB. Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard sqlite3 CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc. While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust ( sqlx , rusqlite , and tokio ), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary. Architecture Splitting data into shards In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly. To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards: Consistent hashing: Each key maps to one shard via multi-probe consistent hashing. Per-shard writer with group commit: Each shard has a dedicated writer task fed by a bounded queue. Instead of committing one key at a time, the writer drains a batch of pending writes from the queue and executes them inside a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT transaction. This amortizes transaction and WAL overhead across concurrent clients. Concurrent readers: Reads go directly to a per-shard pool of read-only SQLite connections and can run concurrently with the writer. How much does sharding help? We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x. All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and batch_size = 50 , with the data directory on tmpfs to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections. Workload 1 shard 16 shards HSET only 7,740 ops/s, p99 10.7 ms 25,324 ops/s, p99 8.3 ms 50% HSET , 50% HGET 14,227 ops/s, p99 10.5 ms 29,538 ops/s, p99 8.5 ms HGET only 67,128 ops/s, p99 2.1 ms 70,884 ops/s, p99 2.3 ms With 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention. At 25,324 HSET operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly 1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources. Schema Our services use both plain keys ( SET / GET ) and Redis hashes ( HSET / HGET ) to group blobs by service or feature (for example, HSET prefs userID <json> ). Inside each shard, plain keys live in a blobs table: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blobs ( key TEXT PRIMARY KEY , data BLOB, created_at INTEGER NOT NULL , updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL , expires_at INTEGER , version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 ); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_expires_at ON blobs(expires_at) WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL ; SET writes to blobs . HSET writes to a table for its namespace, blobs_<namespace> , with the same columns. For example, HSET prefs user42 ... stores user42 in blobs_prefs . Expiry is stored in expires_at on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time ( expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ? ), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on expires_at is a partial index ( WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL ), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index. Compression Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production. Here is the compression ratio across one hour of production HSET traffic: HSET payload Sent by the client Stored in SQLite Reduction Average 63.6 KiB 5.5 KiB about 11x p99 935 KiB 59.3 KiB about 16x With SQLite’s default 4 KiB pages, shrinking a 63.6 KiB payload to 5.5 KiB reduces its storage footprint from roughly 16 pages to roughly 2, before accounting for row and index overhead. Fewer pages holding blob data means less pressure on the page cache and less data to write through the WAL and into the database. Durability Because we don’t require strict durability for our specific use case of UI preferences, shards run in WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL . SQLite does not fsync on every transaction commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent committed transactions that have not yet been synced to durable storage, while preserving database consistency. For workloads that want even lower write latency, Blobasaur also supports an optional async_write mode that acknowledges writes as soon as they enter the shard’s memory queue, before the SQLite batch commits. Scaling across machines To scale beyond a single server, Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, making it compatible with standard cluster-aware Redis clients. Like Redis Cluster, the keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots using CRC16 . Each Blobasaur node owns a configured range of slots, and nodes discover each other via gossip. If a client sends a key to the wrong node, the node responds with a MOVED redirect pointing to the owner node. This gives Blobasaur two-level routing: Cluster level: CRC16(key) % 16384 selects the machine. Node level: Multi-probe consistent hashing selects the SQLite shard on that machine. There are some limitations right now. At present, slot assignment is static in config. Live slot rebalancing between running nodes and automatic failover are not implemented yet. Changing the number of shards We chose multi-probe consistent hashing so resharding a node only has to move minimal data, without needing virtual nodes. With naive hash % num_shards , increasing from 4 to 5 shards moves ~80% of keys. With consistent hashing, only ~20% of keys move (the share belonging to the new shard). Resharding is currently an offline operation via the built-in CLI: Stop the server. Run blobasaur shard migrate 4 5 --verify . Update num_shards in config.toml and start the server. The migration tool moves keys whose target shard changed. With --verify , it checks that keys are in the expected shards and reports post-migration row counts. Moving off SSDB We rolled out Blobasaur in a phased deployment strategy: New workloads first: When we launched Kite Terminal mode, we pointed its workspace storage directly at Blobasaur. Dual-write and backfill: For existing workloads like chart preferences, we updated the services to dual-write to both SSDB and Blobasaur while running a background migration for historical keys. Reads went to Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB on a cache miss or error. Cutover: On the client side, the only code change was switching from a single-node Redis client to a Redis Cluster client with the three Blobasaur node IPs. After running dual-writes for a month with zero discrepancies, we turned off SSDB. What we learned along the way Deleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite files Early on, we noticed disk usage only grew, even after millions of keys expired or were deleted. By default, SQLite keeps freed pages on an internal freelist for future writes rather than returning space to the OS. To fix this, we enabled PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL across every shard and added a blobasaur shard vacuum subcommand to reclaim unused freelist pages within a set allocation (128 MB default). Since shrinking the actual database file in WAL mode requires a checkpoint, Blobasaur runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) right after executing an incremental vacuum. Async writes have to be visible to every read When async_write is enabled, a write returns OK while still sitting in the shard’s memory queue waiting for the next batch commit. To preserve read-your-writes consistency, queued writes are also placed in an in-memory pending map that reads check before querying SQLite. During testing, we hit edge cases where certain read and existence-check paths bypassed this pending map or didn’t account for deletes. For example, a DEL followed immediately by a GET could return the old value from SQLite because the queued DEL hadn’t committed yet. We fixed this by storing explicit tombstones in the pending map and routing every read ( GET , HGET , EXISTS , TTL ) through it first. Expiry cleanup has to share the writer In production, our p99 write latency normally sat below 5 ms, but we occasionally saw spikes to 30 to 50 ms. We traced the spikes to the background TTL cleanup task. Initially, the cleanup worker opened its own write connection and ran a single large DELETE statement for all expired rows. That large DELETE contended with the shard’s main writer for SQLite’s single write lock, stalling normal client batches. We fixed this in two ways: routing cleanup batches through the shard’s existing writer connection so they take turns cleanly with client writes, and bounding each pass with cleanup_chunk_size (1,000 rows by default). Since expired rows are already filtered out at read time, spreading physical deletion across smaller chunks eliminated the latency spikes without affecting correctness. In production Our current Blobasaur deployment runs as a three-node (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) cluster. Over a full trading session (09:00 to 15:30), p99 latency across all commands stays around 2 ms on every node, and p50 sits between 250 and 550 µs. Broken down by command, HSET p99 sits around 2 ms, HGET p99 around 1.4 ms, and HDEL p99 mostly under 1 ms. Blobasaur is open source under the AGPLv3 license and available on GitHub @iamd3vil/blobasaur . Find other projects from the Zerodha.tech hacker collective at 4th Cross Labs . rust databases Zerodha © 2026 All rights reserved.

title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
body_text: Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion | Ruby Ruby Install Docs Libraries Contribution Community News English ( en ) Български ( bg ) Deutsch ( de ) English ( en ) Español ( es ) Français ( fr ) Indonesia ( id ) Italiano ( it ) 日本語 ( ja ) 한국어 ( ko ) polski ( pl ) Português ( pt ) Русский ( ru ) Türkçe ( tr ) Українська ( uk ) Tiếng Việt ( vi ) 简体中文 ( zh_cn ) 繁體中文 ( zh_tw ) Install Docs Libraries Contribution Community News News News Security Recent News (RSS) News News Security Recent News (RSS) Table of Contents Table of Contents Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion Posted by mame on 18 Nov 2026 Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading. CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 : Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x : Double free in regular expression compilation Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px : Integer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w : Heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4 : Heap buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s . Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process. Affected versions Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9 Recommended action We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14. Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes. It found one issue that was easy to fix, simple oversight with a one line fix, so I just went along with it. Then it got stopped because of bullshit “AI safeguards”. Oh no, how dare I , the senior product engineer with my product that I provably have control over, try to fix and prevent security issues and ensure compliance with local laws and regulations? “Oh but you can just apply to get an exemption from them here bla bla fucking blah ” Have you READ the requirements? First of all, you will have to wait for multiple business days to get a response. You forfeit any data retention exemptions, so hope you don’t have any IP to protect! Oh, and oh so please give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise! WHAT. And you may just get fucked anyway and not get approval. Approval to appropriately protect your own service! This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I try to keep up with the security landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is a big fucking no-no and I can’t let that happen. If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck off and use an older model that still will try to stop you from applying adequate protection. You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models. You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special? Predictably, the only way to actually make our own service more secure ended up involving the use of EU-hosted open weights models, such as GLM 5.3, that actually complied with our intentions, proved that the issue is there, and then helped fix and verify that the issue is now resolved, for good. Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place. title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
body_text:
15 million web servers on one VM - smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP Â· kapteko Skip to content kapteko Articles About me 15 million web servers on one VM - smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP Nov 18, 2026 Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there arenât enough web servers for everyone. Letâs run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldnât get funding, so weâre bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, Iâll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and weâll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all. Web server Instead of vibe coding it all, letâs use an ancient technique called learning . First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls. listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket accept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket recv - receives data from a socket send - sends data close - closes What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Letâs use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK . int main ( void ) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket ( AF_INET , SOCK_STREAM , 0 ); if ( listen ( server , 128 ) < 0 ) return 1 ; const char reply [] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK 
 Content-Length: 2 

 OK" ; for ( int client ; ( client = accept ( server , NULL , NULL )) >= 0 ;) { if ( recv ( client , NULL , 4096 , MSG_TRUNC ) > 0 ) send ( client , reply , sizeof reply - 1 , MSG_NOSIGNAL ); close ( client ); } } It couldnât be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that weâve learned everything, letâs finish the article and call it a day: $ for i in $( seq 1 15_000_000 ); do echo $i ; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1 Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0 , so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range . $ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999 Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80) , Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small. Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/ ). Ports 1-1024 require root. Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX. Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading. Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535 , but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server. The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16 , so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses! UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software? Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP , which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range: // Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param ( argv [ 1 ]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x 0a400001 ; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl ( first_ip + i ); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2 And now we can finally finish the article. $ for i in $( seq 1 15_000_000 ); do echo $i ; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memory Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget. Runtime By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust , I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task. TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS. Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly? Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop. for ( int client ; ( client = accept ( server , NULL , NULL )) >= 0 ;) { if ( recv ( client , NULL , 4096 , MSG_TRUNC ) > 0 ) send ( client , reply , sizeof reply - 1 , MSG_NOSIGNAL ); close ( client ); } This code has only two state variables, server and client . Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state: struct Context { pc : u64 , // Instruction address to return to fd_server : i32 , // server file descriptor fd_client : i32 , // client file descriptor } We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32 , and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need? $ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kb Hereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment. 14M idle connections - 0 bytes Scheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB 1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GB Only half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it: int main ( void ) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for ( int i = 0 ; i < 14_000_000 ; i ++ ) { int server = socket ( AF_INET , SOCK_STREAM , 0 ); listen ( server , 1 ) } } $ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid? Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel. Networking in the kernel Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it: int main ( void ) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < 10_000_000 ; ++ i ) { socket ( AF_INET , SOCK_STREAM , 0 ); } } That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes: Struct sizeof Description struct tcp_sock 2240B TCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeeping struct socket_alloc 768B A 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and padding struct file 184B Open-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socket struct dentry 192B The sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeeping Total 3384B Potato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300] , but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel? What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW! The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest? Clear. Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it. HTTP Application Â· L7 TCP Transport Â· L4 IP Network Â· L3 Ethernet Data link Â· L2 Physical L1 GET / Payload Payload Payload â¡ ð© Src port 50123 Dst port 80 Seq 1001 ACK 7001 Flags ACK Src IP 192.0. 2.10 Dst IP 198.51. 100.20 TTL 64 Protocol 6 (TCP) Dst MAC 02:00:00: 00:00:fe Src MAC 02:00:00: 00:00:01 EtherType 0x0800 (IPv4) FCS CRC TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work. There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though: gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stack Seastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDB lwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IP F-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stack Go, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp , which is purely amazing: >smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at all So, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways: TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer TAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer DPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel smoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use. fn main () -> std :: io :: Result < () > { let ( mut device , config ) = match std :: env :: args () . nth ( 1 ) . as_deref () { Some ( "tun" ) => ( TunTapInterface :: new ( "smoltun" , Medium :: Ip ) ? , Config :: new ( HardwareAddress :: Ip ), ), Some ( "tap" ) => ( TunTapInterface :: new ( "smoltap" , Medium :: Ethernet ) ? , Config :: new ( EthernetAddress ([ 0x02 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 2 ]) . into ()), ), _ => panic! ( "pass tun or tap" ), }; let mut iface = Interface :: new ( config , & mut device , Instant :: now ()); iface . update_ip_addrs ( | addrs | { addrs . push ( IpCidr :: new ( IpAddress :: v4 ( 192 , 0 , 2 , 2 ), 24 )) . unwrap (); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet :: new ( Vec :: new ()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant :: now (); iface . poll ( now , & mut device , & mut sockets ); wait ( device . as_raw_fd (), iface . poll_delay ( now , & sockets )) ? ; } } But what about the third option, DPDK ? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet. DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there. Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock , and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost. DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that: loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network (); receive_from_network_to_app_memory (); } Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig , if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that. Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL , which is even closer to DPDK : you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage). To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp , we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us. Now the final flow is: The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memory The runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by one Guest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adapters All 15M guests start listening, each on its own address The scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the next And now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp , RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it: Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster. Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article. References https://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers source https://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDK https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation site https://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview â All articles Articles Â· About me
