How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40k staff
body_text: How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40,000 staff All Government Engineering Security Get Started All Government Engineering Security Get Started How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40,000 staff November 19, 2026 Digital sovereignty The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element, and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users. At The Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it. Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit “Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing. For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control. Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet) With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions. Hosting. The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms. Identity. The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar. Federation. Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change. Nine months from proof of concept to every Commission laptop The Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly: December 2025: the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present. January to June 2026: the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June. Pilots: a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform. July to September 2026: the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September. The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like. Scaling to 40,000 users brought challenges Rolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each. Finding colleagues across servers. The Commission runs several Synapse homeservers, and early on, people on different servers couldn't always find each other. The Commission's teams worked with Element to fix this, and now a plain user search finds anyone in the Commission, whichever server they're on. Accounts that only appear after sign-up. The Commission chose user-led account creation rather than pre-provisioning every account. The catch is that you can't find a colleague who hasn't registered yet, which made the discovery problem above feel worse while adoption was still ramping up. Live presence was switched off. As more users came on board, the load from live presence (the real-time “online/away” indicator) started to affect performance, so the team disabled it. They're now looking at a user status feature being developed with Element as the replacement. Infrastructure had to learn to scale itself. Rolling out in waves over three months meant uneven, shifting demand, so the team tuned the infrastructure to adjust automatically. Running through all of this was the balance between security and usability. Most of the hardening work was done with the Commission's security teams before the rollout, and continues through regular security reviews and continuous improvements. The team made sure that hardening didn't get in the way of everyday tasks like creating an account, recovering it or verifying a new device, and documented those steps clearly for staff. Feedback from tickets, internal forums and public channels is consolidated into prioritised goals for the Commission's own roadmap. Element complements the Commission's toolset The most common question, Diana said, is whether Element is meant to replace Microsoft Teams, or consumer apps like Signal and WhatsApp. The short answer: neither, directly. Element is positioned as an internal communication tool for specific use cases - secure communication among them - where the Commission's existing stack doesn't fully meet its needs. Teams bundles communication, collaboration and a whole platform behind it, so there's no one-to-one swap to be had. That makes expectation-setting part of the job. People naturally compare workplace tools with the apps they use at home and go looking for feature-for-feature matches. Diana's view is that this mindset is something to address head-on in any organisational change: Element is a tool in its own right, with its own feature set, that the Commission and Element can evolve together. Part of the goal is to bring work conversations onto a tool the Commission controls.  Federation goes beyond tech The Commission has been interested in federation for a long time. The obvious starting point is other EU institutions, but it wouldn't stop there: the Commission also works closely with member states, governments and non-governmental organisations. No decision has been made yet, and the Commission is taking it one step at a time. First comes the technical question of what the technology can actually do, because, as Diana put it, there's no point writing policies technology can't deliver. Then comes governance: who the partners would be, on what terms, with what scope, and how security and privacy are handled. The Commission's Takeaways Alexandru ended the talk by sharing what the deployment had taught the Commission. Sovereignty is operational. It depends on operational control and the trustworthiness of the whole chain of partners, not just on where the service is hosted. Adoption depends on everyday usability. Discoverability, onboarding support and everything around the product shape whether people use it. Interoperability needs more than technology. It also needs clear structure, participation and governance. He also noted that introducing a new communication tool has been a journey, and still is. Along the way, the Commission has relied on trustworthy service providers, and he described the collaboration with Element as a success. The live demo was a proof point of what governments can do with the Matrix open standard. title: We need smart people who give a shit
body_text: 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit • VioletPixel VioletPixel Justin Michael's notions and miscellanea Blog About Now Contact Feed Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions. When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable. The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things: Intimate knowledge of the system The drive and determination to force the system to work Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure. Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse. And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365 , Air Traffic Control , United Airlines' systems , the NSA's network , many major banks , Apple's systems , and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI. I guess that depends on how you look at it. I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit. So where did they go? Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity. Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea. People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from? It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics. Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this. It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real. Thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system). We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a big problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail. I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now. Unfortunately, we're all getting burned.
